Sign it please.” But this thing about the beat – I hate to tell you something that’s so important to me – Russell. Come here a second. I need your help. And Chris, you could come.
[interview interrupted by phone call]
Who was in government that was important?
Shultz.
What’s his first . . .? – George.
George Shultz.
Yeah. Well, I can tell you. Close the door.
The next day, we were going to the ballet.

Iola was in line to go to the ballet. I had to do interviews where there was just every – ABC, NBC, Fox – just lines of guys interviewing you from a balcony over Red Square. So I was stuck there. I said, “I won’t be able to get into the ballet. Look at that line.” “We’ll get you in.” So I’m the only guy that gets past the line. I’m in there in an empty lobby. Everybody else is outside. Pretty quick, a phalanx of guards come in. In this part of the phalanx is George Shultz. I’m shoved to the back end of that lobby. George went through the phalanx and came right over to me. He said, “Dave, you saved the meeting – the summit.”
“You saved the summit.” He said, “There was so much tension, but after last night, everything is so much more relaxed.”
I hate not to tell you this, and I’d hate to see it in print and people think, what an ego. But this is what I’m talking about.
Sure, no. It’s an important story.
It is.
Let me ask about other political situations you’ve been involved in. You’ve been involved playing at the White House or presidential events I think going back to the Kennedy administration.
Yeah.
Is that correct?
That’s right.
How do you approach that? How do you play at the White House? Do you play a song? Do you play a set? How do you adapt to that?

A little background to that: Pierre Salinger, whether you know it or not, could have had a career as a classical pianist. He used to come into the Geary Cellar in San Francisco when he was a writer for the [San Francisco] Chronicle. Didn’t he go with one of the girls downstairs?
Yeah. Denise McCluggage.
Do you know who Denise McClugagge is?
No.

She’s the first top great woman race driver. She’s a Mills graduate. She was living [ ] little house downstairs on 18th Street. Pierre would know me. He was Kennedy’s press secretary. Kennedy – every Thursday afternoon he had invited college students and special students that were interested in Washington government to come and live for the summer. We’re finished.
What was this?
George Shultz.
Oh, at the Bolshoi.
Tell them what he said.

This was the day after the summit. After the night of the summit we went from [?] to the Rossiya Hotel, because all the networks had set up. The balcony of the Rossiya overlooks Red Square and St. Basel’s. So it’s “the shot,” to do a live CNN. As Dave came through the corridor on the second floor, every single news organization in the world was set up there. They all came up and applauded Dave, because they’d all seen it. Who was the black anchor for CNN? Bernard . . . [Shaw].
Bernard . . . wonderful guy.

He was the CNN anchor man. Bernard . . . Anyway, does the interview with Dave, finishes it up. He turns to Dave and he says, “Dave, I have to tell you something. Listening to you play Take the ‘A’ Train made me proud to be an American.” He said, “We all were just so emotional at what was taking place.”

The next day, the Bolshoi. It was an all-star gala thing. We were ready to go in, and Shultz comes up. He’s all through the security. He sees Dave. He goes to Dave, through the security line, embraces him, and says, “Dave, you made the summit. Nothing was happening until last night, when everybody looked around and saw that they appreciated the same music.” So that was a pretty emotional evening.
Cultural exchange works.
You were taking about Pierre Salinger.
Thursday afternoon these – pages were a lot of them – . . .
Interns.

. . . interns were invited to the White House. They would not know why they were coming, except it was Kennedy’s afternoon to entertain them. Word got out that I was going to be the entertainment. The lawn at the White House was flooded, and they could not keep that date there, so they moved us to the Washington monument. I don’t remember whether Jack Kennedy came or not.
I don’t think he did.
Bobby was supposed to have been there.
I think there was talk. If he came, he came and went without our knowing it.
Security and all that was changed now. They said, “Would you play a song for Tony Bennett to sing?” I said, “Sure. What’s he want to sing?” Tony, without rehearsals - was it Night and Day?
That Old Black Magic.

That Old Black Magic. It came off just great. It’s on one of my records with different artists. It sounds like we knew what each other was doing. There were thousands and thousands at that, out in the open air. Then the next year – who’d we go for?
Johnson.
Johnson. Oh yeah.
King Hussein.
King Hussein had requested this.

I guess King Hussein was a real jazz fan. So that was the first [ ] group that performed at a state dinner function. They had performed for dances and that sort of thing, but as the entertainer for a state function, it was the first time. From what we understand, it was King Hussein who requested it.
I see. What’s the protocol for that? Do you play a whole set? Do you play just one or two numbers?

You play maybe three or four. The Ellington night, there’s so many jazz musicians that you just go up and play one tune. When I think of the Ellington night, I think of the night that I really liked Dick Nixon, who I hadn’t been a fan of. But he said – we’re at the dinner in a separate room. He gets up to make a speech of welcome. He said, “In this room there’s been welcome and entertainment for kings and queens and leaders of the world, but tonight we entertain our first Duke.” Then he said, “It’s come full circle. Duke’s father was the head” – did he call him . . .
Butler.

“. . . butler in this room. Tonight we’re entertaining and honoring his son.” Isn’t that great? It was so wonderful. Iola was sitting with Mercer [Ellington] in a room full of musicians and great statesmen. I don’t know why I got on that, but I was thinking of how great that was, Duke being raised in Washington.
That’s right. His father catered meals at the White House.
What’d you say?
His father catered meals at the White House.
Yeah, and wasn’t it wonderful of Nixon to bring that . . .
For his birthday.
. . . full circle. Then [Gerald] Ford. He had a train going across the country. We went to the station.
This was ’76, the Freedom Train.
Who else?
There was a [Jimmy] Carter event. Were you at the Carter jazz . . .?
Yeah, in the Rose Garden, Carter.
That’s the night I played with Lionel [Hampton], wasn’t it? Lionel had told us what he’s going to play. He didn’t play one thing that he told us. That great bass player . . .
Ron Carter.
Ron said, “What the heck’s he playing? I don’t know this song.”
That’s right. He played a tune that neither of you had ever played.
Neither of us knew.
If you and Ron don’t know it, it’s got to be a pretty obscure song.
We got through it.

Let me ask about another world figure: Pope John Paul II. You performed Upon this Rock for his visit to San Francisco. You’ve also written a number of other widely performed liturgical works. Can you talk about that aspect of your career?

So many times, like today, I’ll get a phone call for something very important to do. Many times I can’t do it or wouldn’t think it’s appropriate. I can tell you a story about Johnson, President Johnson. I’m in my tomato garden at home, and I am called to come to the phone, saying, “It’s the White House.” I go to the phone. They say, “Dave, we need you to come to . . .”
Thailand.
“. . . Thailand. Can you get on the next plane and come?”
The King of Thailand is a big jazz fan.
He had requested us. I said, “Why? Why do I have to come?” “We’re in big trouble. The President, when he’s seated, is taller than the King is standing. This is
causing such tremendous problems. On top of it, the President has crossed his legs and pointed his shoe at the President” [sic: the King].
The bottom of his shoe.

The bottom of – “We are in big trouble, but we think because the King likes you so much, that if you came and played, it might save the situation.” So I said, “I can’t go. I have other concerts that I have to do during this period.” “Can you think of somebody else that the King would like?” I said, “How about Stan Getz?” “Oh, he’d like that.” I guess I’m talking to his social person.
Social secretary.

So, great. Send Stan. Stan goes all the way there. Didn’t like something that somebody said. Turns around and comes back. Then is talked into going back, and gets on the next plane and goes back. He finally saved the situation. Now we have a friend that’s in Thailand for the King, to teach his kids.
Life is funny, the circles, because one of the Mills girls . . .
That lived downstairs.
. . . that lived on 18th Street in San Francisco ended up being the music teacher for the King of Thailand’s children.
She goes back every year. She might be there now.
Isn’t that crazy?
It’s like The King and I.

That’s funny. I’ve been considering trying to get an interview with the King of Thailand, because I hear he’s a great jazz fan. So I’ve sent these e-mails to the consulate and the ambassador. I tell my wife, “If someone calls and says they’re the King of Thailand on the phone, don’t hang up. It’s not a practical joke.” He hasn’t phoned me back. I’m still hopeful to get an interview at some point.
I kind of got off the track.
That is an interesting story. By all means. We’re moving on. We’re doing world figures now. We’re going to do Pope John Paul II and you writing a work for his visit to San Francisco.

I get a call when I’m in Los Angeles. They call Russell. Russell comes in my room, and said, “The Pope is coming to San Francisco – the diocese in San Francisco. He needs you to write nine minutes for his entrance into Candlestick Park. He will in the Popemobile coming in and circle the park. We don’t have any music ready for that. Could you write something?” I said, “Russell, what do they want me to write?” He said, “They’ve given me one sentence: ‘upon this rock, I will build my church, and the jaws of Hell cannot [ ]’.” I said, “Nine minutes on that? Turn it down.” So he calls back. “Mr. Brubeck thinks he cannot write nine minutes of music for the Pope on that one sentence.” So I go to bed – and this often happens to me. I will dream an answer, because I’m so pent up about this assignment. Bach would write a fugue and could use the words over and over again. I said, “Ask them if they could give me one more sentence? That would help give me more to work with.” So he called back. Everything was going fine. They’ll give me “what is loosed on earth shall be loosed in heaven,” which is . . .
It’s part of the same gospel.

It’s the next sentence. “Which is bound on earth will be bound in heaven.” So I got that sentence, and I started that chorale. I would meet the organist that was the choir director for that – is it called Glass Cathedral, that new cathedral in San Francisco? Not Glass. But it’s beautiful.
The Grace Cathedral.
Not the Grace. It’s a new one.
Because Grace is Episcopal.
It’s a Catholic.
You’re right. It’s not.

So we’re on the way to Japan or Australia, and I said, “If I show the director of the choir, and he’s the person that’s going to be working with this – have him come to the airport in San Francisco and meet us. We’ll go to some room, and I’ll show him the music that I’ve started.” So he meets us there, and I said, “I think I’ve found the solution. I think I’ve written a fugue.” He said, “Let me see it.” He looks at it and sings perfectly the subject, then the counter-subject, then the stretto. “What do you mean, you think you’ve written a fugue? This is a fugue!”, which was good news to hear. So while we’re gone, the bishop, Quinn, is also an organist. He showed the bishop what I’d written. He said, “This is good music, but we’ve had two articles against using Dave, a jazz musician, to perform for the Pope,” very negative articles in both papers. But he

said, “I can defend this music. I’m a musician.” So we get to the part – now I’ve got the quartet. Russell has had one rehearsal with the choir and the musicians. I wrote it for 21 brass and percussion, because outdoors, in a baseball diamond – the altar is on second base, put up like a jigsaw puzzle, just perfectly, very expensive, because they’ve got to put it up and take it down, because there’s a ball game there that night. Can you imagine? It cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. I forget exactly. So [ ] The bishop said, “Dave, don’t use the quartet. The press will kill you. They’ll call it a jazz mass. You’ve written” – he said, “I love your quartet, but I know these guys. Just do the chorale and fugue.” So I brought the group. They were there. They didn’t play a note. You know, he was right, because it’s the narrowness of people that write about things like this to not know that this is America’s music, as Billy – Dr. Billy . . .
Taylor.

Taylor has said, “This is America’s classical music.” This we got to realize, that it’s the basic music of every Broadway show you go to, of rock, of movies – especially in a chase scene. It’s always jazz. Our classical composers that are world-wide known – and this is what Darius Milhaud told me – if you want to express, you have to use the jazz idiom, just as Bartok used the Hungarian folk music, and I’ve used French music, and Bach – Bach used drinking songs. O Sacred Head Now Wounded is a drinking song. Why don’t people realize that almost from the beginning of classical music, they were using folk music and comedy songs. Beethoven, I think, used dance songs that were popular at the time as a point of departure. Over and over. That’s why America has to realize that jazz is the basis of our music, and what’s going to live in our music – like Bernstein, Copland, Gershwin, and Charles Ives have used the jazz idiom. That’s what America should realize. That’s what our teachers, our government, should be thankful that we have such a great music that says in so many words “freedom” to the whole world. This is the expression of freedom, which is the expression of the United States.

Dave, I think I interviewed you back in 1988. At that time I had found an interview you had given in the 1950s in which you had told an interviewer that you would like to spend more time doing classical composition. I mentioned that to you in this 1988 interview, and you said, “I still feel the same way today. I wish I was spending more time doing classical composition.” It seems to me, though, that you have – in the last 20 years, you’ve devoted increasing amounts of time to these compositions. Is there a lot of your music, of compositions that have not been recorded? What is there out there?

The piece that I wrote for the Pope hasn’t been recorded – Upon this Rock – hasn’t been recorded, and I love that piece. It’s a good fugue. It is well-written, as far as I’m concerned. It should have been recorded. But it looks like it will. It’s going to be sung at the Catholic . . .
Notre Dame.

Notre Dame. Maybe someone will record it there. But I know who will record it, will be the Pacific Mozart Chorale, but they’ll record it probably without orchestra – do it a cappella. It would be great if they could record it with orchestra, but that costs a lot of money.
How many works of yours are there that haven’t been recorded? A small number? A large number? What is there in your archives that we haven’t heard?
Have we recorded Chief Seattle?
Not a commercial recording.

Wonderful piece. Chief Seattle spoke to the President of the United States, to the Great Father in Washington. “How can you buy or sell the sky?” Because Washington wanted his land, all of Chief Seattle’s land. There was no way he could stop that from happening. But the speech is one of the greatest speeches on ecology. “Will you teach your children what we have taught our children if I sell you our land? Will you respect the trees, the water, the air, the animals, the fish?” Washington agreed to all of this. Put him on an island off of Seattle, where he could never return to Seattle, where he died. I’ve been to his grave there, with Iola. It was a little frightening to play for the Suquamish tribe Chief Seattle’s speech, because they do not like people to take their music or their texts. So at the first performance, a young chief came and read – what did he read? Part of Chief Seattle? He spoke himself.
He gave the prayer to the four winds, and there was a blessing of the concert.

Then he said, “I have to be gone tomorrow,” because there was a performance the next day, “But I’ll be back.” So he disappeared the next day and came back with an eagle feather that you could smell the smoke where it had been blessed. He gave that to me and said I must wave it when I go to the next world. [ ]
A great-great-great granddaughter of Chief Seattle came to the concert. They were thrilled with it.
It was just the opposite. I was afraid to play my music, do this thing that Iola and I had written. Then we did it live with . . .
Russell Means.
. . . Russell Means, who’s this magnificent man. He was in something you would think of as an American Indian costume, but it wasn’t. He just had the feathers.
His hair was braided.
Braided. He read this with such passion. Do you know much about him?
Just a little.
Because he’s such a powerful force.

He was the head of the AIM, the American Indian Movement. Remember that? They were pretty radical there for a while. Then I think he has done some acting in Hollywood. He is a man of great presence and a very intense, fierce [inaudible].
These are the kind of things that aren’t recorded. The Praise of Mary Canticles haven’t been recorded. These are 35-, 40 minute . . .
These are major compositions of yours that most people haven’t had a chance to hear.
Then this bunch of new things will be recorded.
The Cannery Row work that you performed at Monterey – has that been recorded?
No.
That’s another one that I’ve read reviews of, but haven’t had a chance to hear the music. A lot of people would like to hear this.
It could be . . .
The live performance was recorded, and actually, it’s well enough recorded . . .
It could be commercially released.
I’d love to see that. Clint Eastwood had cameras there. He’s doing a documentary on me.
My next question was going to be to ask you about that.
I keep saying, “Are you going to use Cannery Row?” – through the people in his staff – “Are you going to use Cannery Row in the documentary?” They said, “We’ll use it
as bookends.” I said, “It’s such a good first and only performance, that I would very much like you to do the whole thing.”
That could be an extra feature on the DVD. Now that they have DVDs, they have an extra feature. They could just have the whole performance there.
You just said the answer.
Oh, Is that so? Great minds think alike.
That’s how they answered me. What’d they call it? A bonus.
A bonus feature. That would be great.

“We’ll put it on the end.” They said, “If it’s so important to you, we’d like you to know that we’ve thought of a way. We’ll put it as a complete piece as a bonus.” I don’t know how that works. Maybe you do.
That’ll be great. That will get great visibility. A lot of people will see it.
It will? I’m so anxious to see that.
Just a couple more questions. I’d like to ask you about your marriage. You’ve had – I think you’re going to celebrate your 65th anniversary this year. Is that correct? Is that right?
Isn’t it more?
It may seem like it.
I think it’s 66 coming up.

I just think that’s wonderful. In so many celebrities and musicians, they’re unable to have successful marriages. To see you with such a long, successful marriage and your kids to turn out well. How [ ]? What’s the secret to that success? That’s a great success in its own right, over and above the music.

The secret to everything is one word – love. If you haven’t got that, you’re in trouble. If you have it, you have a chance to be happy. There’s always unhappiness and suffering in this life, but this is what will help you through it all. We’ve had that as the saving of our situation.
Ask my wife.
Iola, do you have any comments on that?

Within the family, it has its ups and downs. There’s strains and everything. But Dave is right, is that underneath there is something that binds you all together. You think of the other person, whether it’s a child or your husband or – but it is as important to you as your own life. If you have those priorities all straight, I think that things work themselves out, if you’re patient and have time and really want them to be resolved. I often quote Dave, because he says, “In music there is no mistake, as long as you can make the resolution.” So that’s kind of the way with life, right? It isn’t a mistake if there is a resolution to whatever the problem is.

I give both of you tremendous credit. I tell you, it’s very inspirational to see. Most people with the kind of fame and career that you’ve had, and to have a stable marriage and the kids turn out the way they have – I give you tremendous credit for that.
Thank you.

I’ve got one last question. The NEA has asked us to do this. They want the people that have been named NEA Masters to give some comments on what it means to them to have been part of the NEA Master program. So any thoughts or observations you have on that would be greatly appreciated.
Joining a group of people that you really respect and honor, then it’s an honor if you’re included in that. That’s the way I feel, that we’ve been very fortunate to be included.

And I think that it has brought to the general public an awareness of the value of the jazz legends, like they did in Washington, D.C., last spring – this spring, wasn’t it? – that, just as in Japan, they have national treasures, that these are our national treasures, that this is our native music. I think that bringing that to the general public – I think the average person now, when they use the term “jazz,” have no idea what they’re talking about, because when you find out, “Oh, you love jazz? Who are some of your favorite players?”, and they all name people that you wouldn’t dream of putting under the classification of jazz. So, I think that’s helped. Then, another area that it’s helped – it has helped people who are trying to start or have a jazz series in a city. I know that it has worked in Arizona. They brought you and the sons in to open a jazz series. They’re selling subscriptions. That brought enough people in that it sustained the subscription. How they did this was calling upon the National Endowment for this backup that is being offered. I’m sure that that’s happened over and

over again, where people who want to sponsor [ ] provide seed money that helps them get started and bring people in, so that they can afford to bring a headliner, and then some of the others they can afford to have on the series. So I think what your brother has done at the National Endowment is giving jazz more recognition than jazz has ever had from any official source.

The Pulitzer Prize in music, for many years they would never give it to a jazz musician, which is a shame when you think of all the great jazz music, and every year they give a Pulitzer Prize in composition. For so many years no jazz musician ever got that. I know Dana wants to use the NEA Jazz Masters to have that kind of – something equivalent to what a Pulitzer Prize in jazz would be. Dave and Iola, I want to thank you. We ran long both days. We told you it would be three hours a day. We did more than four yesterday. We’ve been doing about four today, too. So, thank you very much.
It’s been very pleasant, and I thank you.
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Opening chatter and microphone set-up at Chris Brubeck's house
segments.summary: Brubeck jokes about the house cats and Chris's new studio while the recording gets set up.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Grandfather Louis Warren Brubeck and his hotel in the Nevada desert
segments.summary: Gioia asks about the paternal grandparents; Brubeck tells how his grandfather headed west, built a hotel at the end of a narrow-gauge railroad and was forced out after a shooting and a trial.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Father drives cattle to Concord and meets Henry Ivy
segments.summary: The family moves to the foot of Mt. Diablo around 1896; Brubeck's father hires cowboys from Henry Ivy's livery stable and wins the approval of his future father-in-law.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Few memories of the grandparents; grandfather's funeral
segments.summary: Brubeck hardly knew his grandparents, was kept from his grandfather's funeral at about age five, and mentions the Grass relatives in Santa Cruz.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Uncles Leslie and Phil Brubeck, and the film shown to the tribe
segments.summary: Brubeck describes his father's brothers, especially Phil, who filmed Native Americans and cowboys and whose screening went comically wrong.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Musical ear on father's side and ethnic background
segments.summary: His father whistled classical music by ear; Gioia asks about German, Polish and other ancestry and old-country customs.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Father as cattle buyer and the Depression move to the Ione ranch
segments.summary: Brubeck's father bought cattle across California and then took a job on a 45,000-acre ranch at Ione, to his mother's grief at leaving Concord and her musical life.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Birth at home in Concord, December 1920
segments.summary: He was born at home with Dr. Neff barely arriving in time, and his father was at the Keller ranch slaughterhouse.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Middle names Warren and Keller; rancher Harry Keller
segments.summary: The confusion between David Warren and David Keller Brubeck, and his closeness to cattleman Harry Keller, his father's partner.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: The family home in Concord and the Clayton ranch
segments.summary: The house in town behind the Presbyterian Church where his mother directed the choir, versus the ranch near today's Concord Pavilion where he almost learned to drive.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: His mother's family: Betsy's emigration and organists
segments.summary: Little musical background on his mother's side except some church organists; his grandmother Betsy's route from White Russia and Poland to California.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Mother studies piano in England; her drive and ambitions
segments.summary: His mother, who had helped found Concord High School, cashed in a policy to study in London while the boys were boarded out, and was told by her teacher to go home to her sons.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Mother as first piano teacher; cello and the family string trio
segments.summary: She taught him basic harmony and wrote down what he played; he took up cello, played in a trio with his brothers, and no radio was allowed in the house.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: The Depression: a secure ranch job and hoboes at the door
segments.summary: His father's ranch job gave the family economic security, but Brubeck recalls neighbours losing jobs and hoboes asking for food.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Gil Evans and brother Henry's drumming
segments.summary: Brubeck explains that his brother Henry drummed in Gil Evans's Stockton band and how he finally met Evans at a Miles Davis session.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
segments.title: Early schooling, the slow group and possible dyslexia
segments.summary: He recalls kindergarten, being put in the slow reading group, trouble with spelling and reading music, and his Army IQ score; ends with a short break.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: First paid job with Johnny Osterbar's band at Clements
segments.summary: At about 14 he is invited to play a dance on the Mokelumne River, where rancher Loren Beimert sings, and he describes stock arrangements.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Entering the Stockton musicians union and scale wages
segments.summary: Brubeck, a freshman nobody knew, is brought into the union by Herman Shapiro, lands a $42-a-week club job and earns more than his future father-in-law.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Playing with Cleo Brown in Stockton
segments.summary: He opens, plays intermission and escorts the well-known pianist Cleo Brown, at about age 19.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Wanting to be a cowboy and going to College of the Pacific as pre-med
segments.summary: He did not want college; he left military academy after half an hour, dreamed of the Blakely Ranch, and agreed to study veterinary medicine at Pacific.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Brother Henry's path: Pacific, Dell Courtney, Lompoc job
segments.summary: Henry, 11 and a half years older, left dance bands, finished at Pacific and got a school music job at Lompoc, with a hotcake-breakfast anecdote.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Commuting home to play with Bill Lammi's band; summers with a veterinarian
segments.summary: He plays small-town dances with Lammi, drives a $60 Durant, and hates his summer work putting down dogs.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Roommate's iodine prank and punishment under Dean Corson
segments.summary: Interrupted mid-sentence, he tells of a bathroom fight that ruined a landlady's ceiling and got him moved a mile off campus.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Parents' full names; mother's teaching and choir work after England
segments.summary: Full names of his parents, and how his mother taught from a studio at home, accompanied singers and directed the church choir.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Switching to music; father's offer of partnership on the ranch
segments.summary: A zoology professor sends him to the conservatory; his father says he can always come back to the ranch, and the Birdland owner later laughs at that line.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Lean years in San Francisco: farmer's market produce and Oley's frijoles
segments.summary: In the late 1940s he foraged for cheap food among friends on 18th Street while feeding a young family.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Meeting Iola at the conservatory and the plaque
segments.summary: He first saw Iola Whitlock in a doorway; years later Pacific marked the door with a plaque, and their first conversation was on the radio show Friday Frolic.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Iola's parents, the Whitlocks, and the striped dress he remembered
segments.summary: The Depression and scholarship costs behind Iola's family moving to Stockton, and how he proved he remembered her dress.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Unable to read: the promise never to teach
segments.summary: He dodged keyboard requirements, was nearly refused graduation, and was saved by his harmony and counterpoint teachers on condition he never teach.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Listening: Bach, Debussy, Ravel, Ellington and Kenton
segments.summary: His mother's piano repertoire, his Ellington records from the 1930s and his taste for Gershwin, Bartok and Stravinsky.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Hearing about Pearl Harbor on his 21st birthday
segments.summary: He was visiting his brother Howard in Concord when the news came at a service station.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Postwar plans: working nightclubs and joints
segments.summary: He had planned to keep playing nightclubs, especially jazz places with African-American audiences, and says he would have been happy with that.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Marrying Iola on a three-day Army pass
segments.summary: He arranged a quick wedding in Carson City with no family present, then drove back to camp near Riverside.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: First meeting Duke Ellington and touring with him
segments.summary: He froze backstage in Stockton when introduced to Ellington, who later got him jobs in New York, and years afterward he saw how Duke travelled on tour.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Showing Stan Kenton an arrangement
segments.summary: Kenton tried out Brubeck's score Prayer of the Conquered with his band and said to bring it back in ten years.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Integrated bands: the Wolf Pack and earlier mixed groups
segments.summary: He claims he integrated the Army band and recalls earlier mixed groups, including the octet and a Modesto trio in 1939.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Trying to join black Army and Navy bands at Fort Meade and Washington
segments.summary: Prompted by Gloyd, he tells how he sat in with a black Army band and with Bud Harr's Navy band but was barred from joining either.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Troop ship to Europe, Verdun and forming a band
segments.summary: He crosses on the George Washington, reaches the mud at Verdun, plays for a Red Cross truck show and is kept from the front to lead a band of wounded men.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: The son of the army pianist who took his place
segments.summary: Years later a piano tuner turns out to be the son of the pianist whose job Brubeck took, and Brubeck tells him his father played better than he did.

segments.chapter: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
segments.title: Pearlman, Studs Terkel's The Good War and the Cronkite recording
segments.summary: The man who built the truck changed his name to Waxman and appears in Terkel's book; Brubeck also recorded Private Brubeck Remembers with Walter Cronkite.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Choosing Mills College to study with Milhaud
segments.summary: His brother Howard's studies led him to Milhaud, who told him before the war to come study with him afterward.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Milhaud's class and the birth of the octet
segments.summary: Milhaud invites jazz players to write counterpoint for jazz instrumentation, which becomes the octet with Paul Desmond and Cal Tjader.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Meeting with Arnold Schoenberg
segments.summary: Schoenberg rebukes him for writing a note because it sounds good and shows him cabinets of scores.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Opinion of Schoenberg and twelve-tone writing
segments.summary: He uses twelve-tone rows for melodies but never harmony, noting that The Duke has a row in the bass, and dislikes strict serialism.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Stravinsky's Octet and the idea of Third Stream
segments.summary: He says jazz has always borrowed from classical music, citing Jelly Roll Morton, Tatum and Ellington, and questions the Third Stream label.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Practising at Mills and developing voicings by ear
segments.summary: He did no scales or Hannon, improvised and altered songs, and found his chord voicings by ear; Milhaud once showed him a huge polytonal chart.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Forming the octet and its few gigs
segments.summary: The octet formed in Milhaud's class and played only a handful of concerts; his father called it the damndest noise.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Hardship, family and confidence in the music
segments.summary: He justified the sacrifice to his family by confidence in the music, and compares marriages of musicians such as Paul Desmond's.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: The Marines Memorial concert and how the trio was born
segments.summary: Pressed to put his name on the octet concert, he then gets NBC's Jimmy Lyons and Maria Corbin interested, leading to a trio radio show.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: Awareness of bebop and Parker, Gillespie
segments.summary: He heard no modern jazz during the war and says everyone does what they want, later touring with Parker and playing Birdland.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: San Francisco dixieland scene and son Darius's memory for Turk Murphy
segments.summary: The question of Lu Watters and Turk Murphy leads to a story of young Darius recognizing Murphy's music from a record.

segments.chapter: Mills, Milhaud and the octet
segments.title: End of day one
segments.summary: Gioia notes they have covered up to the start of the trio and stops for the day.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: The Three D's: Darrell Cutler, Don Rattle and Dave Brubeck
segments.summary: Brubeck explains how the Three D's formed from Stockton friends and played standards with singer Francis Lynne.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: First meeting with Paul Desmond at the Presidio audition
segments.summary: Before going overseas he auditioned for a Presidio band where Desmond called his changes wigsville.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Jimmy Lyons, the Geary Cellar and Ralph Gleason's bad review
segments.summary: Lyons broadcast from near the Geary Cellar and championed Brubeck; Gleason panned the Marines Memorial concert but later changed his tune.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Octet concert format and the lost octet library
segments.summary: He describes dividing concerts into classical, jazz and free parts, and the flood in Australia that destroyed Van Kreidt's octet book.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Reconstructing the octet music for Chicago, 2001
segments.summary: Gloyd tells how Neil Tesser and Jeff Levinson transcribed the octet recordings for the 2001 Chicago festival and Avery Fisher Hall, where Lew Soloff found the music hard.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Why the octet music is unique and the lost book
segments.summary: Gioia and Gloyd praise the octet's counterpoint and minimalism and Brubeck regrets the lost manuscripts.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: The Band Box and Paul Desmond's departure to Feather River
segments.summary: Desmond hires away Francis Lynne and Norman Bates for the Band Box, then leaves for Feather River, leaving Brubeck out of work.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Silver Log Tavern, Burma Lounge and opening the Blackhawk
segments.summary: He takes a hot summer job at Clear Lake, then Jimmy Lyons finds him trio work in Oakland and the Blackhawk.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Los Angeles work at the Haig, Mulligan and starting Fantasy recordings
segments.summary: On off-months he plays Gerry Mulligan's club the Haig, and urges the Weiss brothers to record Red Norvo and Mulligan.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Teaching a jazz extension course with Iola; Herb Wong
segments.summary: Iola lectured while Dave played examples in a Berkeley extension class that included young Herb Wong.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Setting up a chair and microphone for Iola
segments.summary: The group sets up a chair and microphone so Iola can join the conversation.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Listing himself as a teacher to get a telephone
segments.summary: Jazz musicians were last on the phone priority list, so Iola's friend advised putting down teacher.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Teaching piano students; Earle Weatherwax
segments.summary: He taught some students and remains in touch with nightclub singer-pianist Earle Weatherwax.

segments.chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
segments.title: Aside about Weatherwax's friend Georgia Frontiere
segments.summary: A side conversation about a wealthy supporter of the Brubeck Institute, with Gioia saying it will be edited out.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Birth of son Darius
segments.summary: Brubeck recounts waiting at the hospital with Bob Skinner, being late for the Geary Cellar, and playing Milhaud for the newborn.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: How Fantasy Records got Brubeck's first recordings
segments.summary: The Weiss brothers bought back his unpaid first masters from a trombonist-label owner and built Fantasy Records on them.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Swimming accident in Honolulu and recovery
segments.summary: Hurt diving, he was in traction for 21 days, ordered to float daily, and suffered lasting back and neck problems.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Weiss brothers and sidemen replace him
segments.summary: He felt betrayed when his sidemen were pressed to find another pianist while he recovered.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Paul Desmond's insistence on joining; letting him into the house
segments.summary: Desmond wanted to play with Brubeck above all, and showed up offering to do chores despite the Feather River betrayal.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: The mysterious $500 in the Honolulu bank account
segments.summary: Broke and unable to fly, he found money in his account to buy ship tickets home, possibly from Doris Duke.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Early quartet recordings and the 'cool' label
segments.summary: He cites a live NBC broadcast of This Can't Be Love and Look for the Silver Lining as hard-swinging, not cool.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: First New York appearance at Birdland and early reviews
segments.summary: Good reviews from John Hammond and Barry Ulanov helped the quartet go to New York.

segments.chapter: Fantasy Records, the accident and the quartet
segments.title: Rehearsing and preparation in the quartet's early years
segments.summary: Most development happened on the job, with rehearsals mainly for new recorded material such as Eurasia.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: From Fantasy to Columbia: first sessions and the Weiss brothers' attitude
segments.summary: The first Fantasy trio session with a faulty Ampex ended in four acetate sides; the Weiss brothers called the music garbage.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: Columbia engineers and three albums a year
segments.summary: Fred Clough engineered many sessions under a Columbia contract requiring three albums a year for 17 years.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: How the themed albums were chosen
segments.summary: Show-tune and songwriter albums arose from suggestions; the Matt Dennis album was his idea via Ken Curtis.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: Freedom at Columbia and royalty mistakes on Time Out
segments.summary: Columbia had to grant artistic freedom, but without a lawyer he lost money on original-composition royalties.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: John Hammond, Cal Lampley and Teo Macero
segments.summary: He had no dealings with Hammond; his sessions with Cal Lampley helped break Teo Macero into jazz production.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: Taking jazz to college campuses
segments.summary: Iola booked colleges by letter, offering student associations guaranteed splits, which made campus concerts viable.

segments.chapter: Columbia years and fame
segments.title: The Time magazine cover and Ellington's knock on the door
segments.summary: The 1954 Time cover brought backlash and benefits, and Duke woke him in Denver with the issue.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Writing The Real Ambassadors in the car
segments.summary: He and Iola wrote the show on pads while waiting during the children's lessons.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Broadway producers decline The Real Ambassadors
segments.summary: Josh Logan and Leland Hayward liked the music, but the Broadway audience was not seen as ready for a show about integration.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: The one performance at Monterey with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: The only staging was at the Monterey Jazz Festival with Armstrong, Carmen McRae and Lambert, Hendricks and Bavan.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Meeting Louis Armstrong in Chicago despite Joe Glaser and Frenchie
segments.summary: Brubeck waited in the hallway until Armstrong invited him to dinner and to sit in; Armstrong later said the show meant a lot to him.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: State Department tour of Poland and Turkey; radio bands
segments.summary: Poland and Turkey were responsive, and European radio bands were steady jobs; a tangent follows on who played with Desmond.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Origin of Blue Rondo a la Turk and Columbia's A-side decision
segments.summary: He heard a 9/8 street rhythm in Turkey, wrote Blue Rondo, and Columbia chose Take Five as the A side.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Joe Morello joins; Desmond's ultimatum
segments.summary: Desmond recommends Morello, then demands he go; Brubeck keeps Morello and Desmond and Bates return.

segments.chapter: Ambassadorship and the quartet's end
segments.title: Disbanding the quartet at the end of 1967
segments.summary: He gave a year's notice, the Huntley-Brinkley Report announced it, and Desmond played his last concert with him.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Moving to Connecticut
segments.summary: What was meant to be a year in Wilton became permanent, thanks to better schools, New York proximity and Irving Townsend's house.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Columbia drops him in 1971
segments.summary: His lawyers learn Columbia dropped him six months earlier; he and Tony Bennett were then invited to play at the Columbia meeting.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Resisting commercial pressure in the 1970s
segments.summary: He says he never made a strictly commercial record except perhaps Red, Hot and Cool.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Electric keyboards
segments.summary: He used a Baldwin electric piano once on Gates of Justice; his sons use synthesizers.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Playing with his sons and the wives' disputes
segments.summary: He reflects on the strains of bandleading with his sons and their marriages.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Growing up with music in the house; Chris's bass
segments.summary: His sons grew up around rehearsals with Mulligan, Morello and Desmond, and Chris sight-read a difficult bass part.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Playing with Gerry Mulligan
segments.summary: Mulligan sat in everywhere; they performed together for decades, including a 1990s European tour.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: George Wein's Mexico festival and finding Jack Six and Alan Dawson
segments.summary: Having just disbanded the quartet, he assembled a new rhythm section for a 1968 festival in Mexico.

segments.chapter: Connecticut, family and collaborators
segments.title: Bravo Brubeck and playing in Mexico
segments.summary: He recorded Bravo Brubeck with Mexican musicians the year before and played cheap park concerts.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Invited to the Reagan-Gorbachev summit in Moscow
segments.summary: Glasnost, the guest list and the stifling curtained room where he was to play.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: The jazz beat in the room and catatonic patients responding to live music
segments.summary: The room warmed to the beat, which recalls an Army hospital where live jazz drew responses from catatonic patients.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Duet with Eugene Wright before Gorbachev and Reagan
segments.summary: Wright came through the door over Gorbachev's table with his bass, and Gorbachev's interpreter asked Brubeck to sign his Kremlin pass.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: George Shultz says Brubeck saved the summit
segments.summary: After a phone-call interruption, Brubeck tells how Shultz thanked him at the ballet for easing tension.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: How Pierre Salinger got him to play for the Kennedy White House
segments.summary: Salinger, a pianist and writer who knew him from the Geary Cellar, connected him to Kennedy's intern events.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Bernard Shaw and Shultz at the Bolshoi, as told by Gloyd
segments.summary: Gloyd recounts the news crews applauding Brubeck and Shultz embracing him at the Bolshoi.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Playing for White House interns with Tony Bennett
segments.summary: The Kennedy-era concert moved to the Washington Monument, and Bennett sang That Old Black Magic without rehearsal.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: State dinner for King Hussein under Johnson
segments.summary: Brubeck's group was the first jazz entertainment at a White House state dinner, at Hussein's request.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Nixon's Ellington birthday night
segments.summary: Nixon's speech that Duke's father had been a butler in the White House moved Brubeck.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: Ford's Freedom Train and Carter's Rose Garden with Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: Brief recollections of performances for Ford and Carter, where Hampton played an unknown tune.

segments.chapter: White House and Kremlin performances
segments.title: President Johnson's call about the King of Thailand
segments.summary: Brubeck recommends Stan Getz to soothe the Thai king after protocol blunders.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Writing Upon This Rock for Pope John Paul II
segments.summary: He wrote a fugue for 21 brass and percussion for the pope's Candlestick Park entrance, and the bishop advised leaving out his quartet.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Jazz as America's classical music
segments.summary: He argues jazz is the basis of American music and that composers have always used popular idioms.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Unrecorded compositions in the archives
segments.summary: Upon This Rock and other works remain unrecorded.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Chief Seattle and Russell Means
segments.summary: He recounts performing his Chief Seattle piece for the Suquamish tribe with Russell Means narrating.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Praise of Mary, Cannery Row and the Clint Eastwood documentary
segments.summary: Major unrecorded works and plans to include Cannery Row as a bonus in the Eastwood film.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: The secret of a long marriage
segments.summary: Brubeck says the secret is love; Iola adds that resolution matters as in music.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: What the NEA Jazz Masters honor means
segments.summary: Brubeck and Iola comment on the value of the NEA program.

segments.chapter: Compositions and closing reflections
segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Gioia thanks them after long sessions.
